episodes.title: Killing of Leroy Mitchell
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The killing of Leroy Mitchell was the shooting of a Black man by a white man near Alton, Halifax County, Virginia, in mid-August 1920, after a posse trailed him on an accusation that he had attempted to attack a white girl. Mitchell died of shotgun wounds, and no arrest had been reported a week later. White papers carried the Associated Press account of a brother avenging his sister, while the Chicago Defender reported that Mitchell had only tipped his hat to the girl.

episodes.title: Alamance County jail shooting
episodes.doubt: mob attack on the jail contested (troops vs citizens/grand jury); James Ray, a white crowd member (B-T 5346 'coincidental death'), was killed by the guard
episodes.summary: The Alamance County jail shooting was the killing of James Ray and the wounding of two other men on the night of July 19, 1920, when a Durham machine-gun company guarding three Black prisoners in the jail at Graham, North Carolina, against a threatened lynching fired into a crowd. The soldiers said a mob fired on them first; Governor Thomas W. Bickett's committee upheld them, while the county grand jury found no mob and no provocation. Black newspapers praised Bickett for saving the prisoners.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Jeffress
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Jeffress took place on August 25, 1920, near Graham, North Carolina, when a mob took the Black prisoner from Sheriff C. D. Story and his deputies on the way to court and shot him outside town. He had been arrested that morning, charged with attacking a young white girl, and a grand jury had already indicted him. The killing came a month after machine gunners had turned back a mob at the same jail, and it led to calls for the sheriff's removal.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Will Morrison from Coulterville, Illinois
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Will Morrison from Coulterville, Illinois, took place on August 16, 1920, when unidentified persons burned the home of Morrison, a Black mine employee, and forced him out of the Randolph County mining town. The burning followed a walkout by white miners who would not work with him, and several Black families were reported to have left afterward. Some papers reported a "race riot" with shooting, which town officials denied.

episodes.title: Avoyelles Parish night riding, 1920
episodes.summary: The Avoyelles Parish night riding of 1920 was a campaign by night riders who drove Black residents away from several communities in Avoyelles Parish, Louisiana, on or before August 15, 1920. No deaths or injuries were reported, and a meeting of more than two hundred men denounced the practice. The only known account appeared in the Dallas Express, a Black weekly.

episodes.title: Kinston jail lynching plot (1920)
episodes.summary: The Kinston jail lynching plot was a reported plan in early August 1920 by a group of a score or more people to kill three Black prisoners held in the county jail at Kinston, North Carolina, before they could be tried. Officials moved one of the men, Joseph Franklin, out of the county and on to Raleigh, and no one was reported harmed. The story reached readers only through a Black wire dispatch, which Black weeklies headlined as a lynching attempt that had been balked or "outwitted".

episodes.title: Chicago Heights race-riot scare
episodes.doubt: riot denied by officials and the Black press; one reported fight at a Black family's house
episodes.summary: The Chicago Heights race-riot scare was a period of reported conflict between Italian and Black residents of Chicago Heights, Illinois, in early August 1920, during which deputy sheriffs patrolled the town and a National Guard company was mobilized. Wire services reported rioting and a Black exodus, but the police chief, the mayor and the Black press called the reports exaggerated or false. The episode became chiefly a dispute over the press, with the Chicago Whip charging that a Hearst daily had invented it.

episodes.title: Police beating of Claude Cheeks
episodes.doubt: race not stated (Black-press local columns only); beating in custody per the Whip, denied in the officers' version
episodes.summary: The police beating of Claude Cheeks was an incident in Chicago in late July or early August 1920 in which Cheeks, a 36-year-old South Side resident, suffered severe head injuries while in the hands of police. The Chicago Whip reported that he was beaten by several officers while under arrest, while the Chicago Defender carried the officers' version that he had fired on them and injured himself while fleeing.

episodes.title: Police shooting of James Jackson
episodes.doubt: race not stated; Black-press columns mark whites '(white)' and leave Jackson unmarked
episodes.summary: The police shooting of James Jackson took place in Chicago on or about July 30, 1920, when detective-bureau sergeants shot the 22-year-old as he tried to get away from them. Jackson was left in critical condition in the County hospital, and two of the city's Black weeklies, the Chicago Whip and the Chicago Defender, reported the shooting in their police columns.

episodes.title: Bombing of 4660 Prairie Avenue
episodes.summary: The bombing of 4660 Prairie Avenue was an attack on an apartment building in Chicago, Illinois, into which a Black family, "the only Negro family in the block," was moving in the summer of 1920. A bomb exploded beneath the front stairway before the family had finished moving in, demolishing the front of the building but injuring no one. The only account found is a short item in the Colorado Statesman, which headlined it as a bombing "by whites."

episodes.title: Bombing of the Jackson home on East 48th Street, Chicago
episodes.summary: The bombing of the Jackson home on East 48th Street was an attack in Chicago on a house occupied by a Black couple, Mr. and Mrs. J. Jackson, by men who threw a bomb from a passing car shortly after midnight on a Sunday in early August 1920. The bomb broke windows but injured no one, and the bombers escaped. Two Chicago Black weeklies treated it as part of a series of bombings and faulted the authorities.

episodes.title: 35th and Wabash police shooting
episodes.summary: The 35th and Wabash police shooting took place on the evening of August 20, 1920, in Chicago, when a white policeman described as drunk fired at a Black man after a traffic quarrel at 35th Street and Wabash Avenue. The shots missed, the man disarmed the officer, and a second policeman had him taken away. Two Chicago Black weeklies reported it the next day; the Chicago Whip said he "came near causing a riot."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Sergeant
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of James Sergeant took place on the night of August 11, 1920, in Hoboken, New Jersey, when a crowd beat Sergeant, a Black man of 21, and chased him into a motion picture theatre shouting "Lynch him!" Police held the crowd off with drawn revolvers until reserves arrived, and Sergeant was taken to headquarters and charged with disorderly conduct. New York dailies reported it the next day under headlines about a lynching averted, and the Chicago Whip carried a short report a week later.

episodes.title: Fitzgerald church picnic shooting
episodes.doubt: single Black-press report; crowd's race and the race of those hurt not stated; the shooter was the white man with the colored woman
episodes.summary: The Fitzgerald church picnic shooting was a clash at a church picnic in Fitzgerald, Georgia, reported in August 1920, in which a crowd took a Black woman away from the white man accompanying her. The man drew a revolver and fired, and in what was described as a "near riot" one man was shot and several people were hurt. The episode is known from a single brief item in the Chicago Broad Ax.

episodes.title: Killing of Leslie Allen
episodes.summary: The killing of Leslie Allen was the shooting death of a 22-year-old Black hotel porter by a posse of Halifax County citizens near Virgilina, Virginia, on the morning of August 26, 1920. Allen had been accused of insulting two white girls at the Buffalo Hotel and of shooting James Baptist, a white man who tried to seize him. Some papers headlined the killing as a lynching, and one reported that the governor of Virginia would investigate.

episodes.title: Expulsion of R. Baxter McRary from Lexington, North Carolina
episodes.summary: The expulsion of R. Baxter McRary was the forced departure of a wealthy Black real estate dealer and Masonic grand master from Lexington, North Carolina, in August 1920, after white citizens found him hiding beneath the home of editor H. B. Varner. After a night in jail he was told through the mayor to leave town or risk his safety, and he left. Varner then sued him for $100,000, and Black papers asked why McRary had not been lynched and whether the affair was a scheme to take his wealth.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Williams
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Robert Williams took place at the city jail in Lynchburg, Virginia, at about 1 a.m. on August 15, 1920, when a crowd of 200 to 300 or more tried to seize Williams, a Black man accused of assaulting Annie Ross, a Swedish-born masseuse. Police had already moved Williams out of the jail, and officers dispersed the crowd and arrested two men, who were fined and jailed for unlawful assembly and riot. In September a jury convicted Williams after eight minutes and he was sentenced to death.

episodes.title: Lynching of Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicut
episodes.summary: The lynching of Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicut took place in Corinth, Alcorn County, Mississippi, on the night of August 27–28, 1920, when a mob of 75 to 100 men forced the jailer to surrender his keys and hanged the two Black prisoners from a telegraph pole. The men, escaped chain-gang prisoners who had surrendered, were accused of striking down a guard. The county prosecuting attorney declared that "at least one" was innocent, and the guard was reported to have said neither had attacked him, a report his son disputed.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Scott Garner
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Scott Garner took place in Anderson, South Carolina, on the night of about July 27, 1920, when a crowd gathered to seize a 14-year-old Black youth arrested on an accusation of attacking a white woman. Officers drew the crowd off with a decoy automobile while a deputy sheriff took Garner out of the city, reportedly toward Columbia. The episode survives in a single dispatch headlined "Probable Lynching Averted."

episodes.title: Warrenton manhunt for Andrew Jackson
episodes.summary: The Warrenton manhunt for Andrew Jackson was an armed search by posses of more than 200 men for Andrew Jackson, alias Andrew Fields, a Black prisoner who escaped from the jail at Warrenton, Virginia, on August 9, 1920. The Washington Times reported open threats to lynch him, but he was back in jail within days and the town's mayor denied that any mob had threatened.

episodes.title: Arcadia moonshine raid shooting
episodes.summary: The Arcadia moonshine raid shooting took place on the morning of 28 August 1920, when four Oklahoma County and federal officers raided the home of Charles Chandler, a Black farmer, near Arcadia in Logan County, Oklahoma, in search of a still. Chandler, Deputy Sheriff Homer Adrean and federal prohibition officer Stanley F. Weiss were killed, Deputy Claude Tyler was wounded, and Chandler's son was shot and arrested. Who shot whom was never settled in the coverage, and the son's lynching the next night drew the Black press to the case.

episodes.title: Lynching of Claude Chandler
episodes.summary: The lynching of Claude Chandler took place on the night of August 29, 1920, when masked men took Chandler, a 19-year-old Black prisoner, from the Oklahoma County jail in Oklahoma City and hanged him west of the city. He was accused of killing two officers in a raid on his father's home near Arcadia. Governor J. B. A. Robertson charged that officers had colluded with the mob, and reports of armed Black men raised fears of a race riot.

episodes.title: Death of Herbert Brooks
episodes.doubt: completed lynching rests on the Bahamian residents' charge, denied by officers and autopsy; a crowd of 1,200 demanded Brooks at the jail (B-T 'possible lynching')
episodes.summary: The death of Herbert Brooks occurred on July 31, 1920, when Brooks, a Black Bahamian held on a charge of assaulting an elderly white woman in Miami, Florida, died near Ormond while officers were taking him by train to Jacksonville. Officials said he leaped from the train, but Bahamian residents of Miami said he had been lynched, and their protest led the mayor to call out the National Guard. An autopsy demanded by the British vice-consul was reported to find nothing to support that charge, and Black papers added their own comment to the wire story.

episodes.title: Killing of Buck Beale
episodes.summary: The killing of Buck Beale was the death of a young Black man in a fight with a sheriff and a posse of fifteen citizens at his home ten miles west of Jefferson, Texas, on the night of Saturday, August 7, 1920. The posse had gone after Beale on an accusation that he had attacked a young white woman, a charge the dispatch stated as fact. An Associated Press brief carried the story to papers in Oklahoma, Arkansas and Texas, several of which headlined it as the killing of an attacker of a white woman.

episodes.title: Lynching of Monroe Wood
episodes.doubt: single rumor-style report reaching Dothan; no follow-up found
episodes.summary: The lynching of Monroe Wood was the reported killing of a Black man by a mob near Newville, Henry County, Alabama, in early August 1920. Wood was accused of insulting a white woman, and the only account, a secondhand report carried by the Montgomery Advertiser, said he was caught and shot to death.

episodes.title: Walnut Cove carnival dance shooting
episodes.doubt: Martin called white by two papers, a negro by one; the Black man was wounded, not killed
episodes.summary: The Walnut Cove carnival dance shooting was a gun battle on August 22, 1920, on a road about a mile north of Walnut Cove, North Carolina, between a sheriff's posse and three escaped prisoners from Madison, one of them a Black man, who had been arrested after a row at a carnival dance hall. Chief of Police Matthews of Walnut Cove and Walter Martin, one of the prisoners, were killed, and the unnamed Black man was seriously wounded and escaped. The Associated Press traced the trouble to the Black man's reported insistence on dancing with white girls, and the story ran in papers across the country under headlines such as "Race Riot in South."

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Roach
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ed Roach was the killing of a Black laborer by a mob that took him from the Person County jail near Roxboro, North Carolina, in late July 1920, after he was charged with attempting to assault a white girl. Soon afterward his white employer, the contractor Nello Teer, published a letter stating that Roach had been at work when the crime was committed. The case drew editorial comment across the country as a lynching of an innocent man, and Governor Bickett offered rewards for the arrest of each member of the mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Spencer
episodes.summary: The lynching of James Spencer was the killing of a Black railway postal clerk by masked men near Basic City, Mississippi, in the summer of 1920, while an officer was taking him to answer a charge of assaulting a white fellow clerk. Lauderdale County's new circuit judge, C. C. Miller, singled out the case in his charge to the grand jury in August, but the grand jury reported that it could not find evidence to indict anyone for the county's mob violence.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lige Daniels
episodes.summary: The lynching of Lige Daniels took place on August 2, 1920, at Center, Texas, when a mob of more than a thousand men stormed the county jail and hanged Daniels, a Black man charged with murdering a white woman, from a tree in the courthouse yard. It followed the officers' announcement of his confession and came although the governor's office had ordered a cavalry company to protect him. The NAACP protested to Governor W. P. Hobby, counting it the eighth Texas lynching of the year, and a Black weekly reported that the sheriff gave the mob the keys.

episodes.title: Attempted lynchings of Percy Thompson and Ludie Martin
episodes.summary: The attempted lynchings of Percy Thompson and Ludie Martin were attempts in the summer of 1920 by mobs of white men to force the Lauderdale County jail at Meridian, Mississippi, and seize two Black prisoners. Officers turned back the mob that came for Thompson, who was later convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. The attempts drew notice chiefly through a new circuit judge's charge to the grand jury, reported under the headline "Grand Jury Told to Go After Mob."

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Esserville, Virginia
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Black residents from Esserville, Virginia, took place in early August 1920, when nearly all of the town's Black population left after an order to 'clear out' that followed the killing of a white policeman named Wilson. Only three Black persons or families were reported to remain, and the town's mayor and the county solicitor appealed without success for the others to return. The episode was reported only in the Black press, which attributed the order variously to the Ku Klux, a band of masked men, or a 'citizens' committee'.

episodes.title: Kidnapping of Jesse Jones and Eugene Stroman
episodes.summary: The kidnapping of Jesse Jones and Eugene Stroman was the night seizure, on July 22, 1920, of two Black farm hands near Wadesboro, Anson County, North Carolina, by three white men from Bamberg County, South Carolina, who carried them handcuffed across the state line. The planter W. D. Mayfield, who led the party, had accused the two of selling mortgaged property, and North Carolina's governor had refused to return them. The "Mayfield kidnapping case" became a two-month extradition contest between the governors and ended with guilty pleas and fines at Wadesboro.

episodes.title: Alleged whipping of Champion Jones
episodes.doubt: whipping contested: no marks found; constable says he kept custody and took the men to be Black
episodes.summary: The alleged whipping of Champion Jones was a reported flogging of a Black prisoner by masked white men near Pamplico, South Carolina, on the night of July 31, 1920, as a constable was driving him to the Florence county jail. The claim, made by the prisoner, was contradicted by a physician who found no whipping marks and by the constable, who said he drove off the men.

episodes.title: Lynching of Herman and Irvin Arthur
episodes.summary: The lynching of Herman and Irvin Arthur was the burning of two Black brothers by a white mob at Paris, Lamar County, Texas, on July 6, 1920, after they were accused of killing a white farmer and his son. A special grand jury indicted five persons for first-degree murder, but no report of an arrest or trial appears in the coverage. Black newspapers covered it first through the indictments and then through a Paris resident's letter released by the NAACP.

episodes.title: Vineland manhunt
episodes.summary: The Vineland manhunt was a three-day pursuit in August 1920 by posses of white residents of Jefferson County, Missouri, after a Black man accused of attempting to attack a white girl, Gertrude Wilson, near Vineland on August 11. The man, who gave his name as David Robinson of Chicago, was shot and wounded, captured near Blackwell on August 14, and jailed at Hillsboro rather than lynched. Wire services carried the hunt nationally, one headline announcing a search 'to lynch him'.

episodes.title: Ensley Alley H house dynamiting
episodes.doubt: police say a Black estranged husband (McShants) confessed; unverified; ANP says second blast in two weeks
episodes.summary: The Ensley Alley H house dynamiting was the bombing of a house occupied by Black residents at Alley H and Twenty-first street in Ensley, Alabama, on Thursday, August 19, 1920. The blast wrecked the house and injured two of its occupants, but no one was killed. The Birmingham Age-Herald first presented it as one of a series of unsolved dynamitings, then reported that police had arrested a Black man who blew up the house to avenge himself on his estranged wife, while a Black-press wire brief said the dynamiters had not been caught.

episodes.title: Coney Island train assault by sailors (1920)
episodes.summary: The Coney Island train assault was an attack on the night of August 5, 1920, in which a group of United States sailors beat five Black passengers on a Brooklyn Rapid Transit (B.R.T.) train leaving Coney Island and threw them off the train. A white boy selling peanuts who protested was also beaten and thrown off, and the sailors were never identified by the victims. The New York Age reported the attack as a Southern-style "outrage" in New York, and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People took up the case.

episodes.title: Arrest of a railroad labor agent at Canton, Mississippi
episodes.summary: The arrest of a railroad labor agent at Canton, Mississippi, took place in August 1920, when local authorities arrested an unnamed Black man employed by the Illinois Central Railroad to secure labor. According to the Chicago Whip, he was held incommunicado after a "mock trial" and fined $500, to be worked out on a peonage farm. The Whip presented the case as an attempt to stop Black migration from the state and reported that people were leaving Canton by night in response.

episodes.title: Peonage and disappearance of Cornelius Alexander
episodes.doubt: death presumed from an exhumed body; cause and killers not reported
episodes.summary: The peonage and disappearance of Cornelius Alexander was a 1920 case in Pike County, Georgia, in which a Black laborer held to work off a debt went missing and federal investigators exhumed a body identified as his near Holtinsville. Members of the white Connell family were indicted for peonage, and the New York Age presented the case as proof that slavery survived in Georgia.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ely Thomas and Tim Zachary
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Ely Thomas and Tim Zachary occurred on August 9, 1920, when a mob from Calhoun, Oklahoma, marched on the Le Flore County jail at Poteau to hang the two Black prisoners. Sheriff Fred Carter and his deputies drove both men out of town before the mob reached them, and they were lodged in the state penitentiary at McAlester. Thomas was convicted of murder less than a month later and sentenced to death.

episodes.title: Greenville, North Carolina, police shooting of 1920
episodes.summary: The Greenville, North Carolina, police shooting of 1920 was an incident in which Lester Jones, chief of police in Greenville, N. C., fired into an automobile carrying four Black people when its driver did not stop at his order to halt. Two of the occupants were injured, and the chief's stated reason was that he "supposed" the car contained liquor. The shooting was reported by the Associated Negro Press and carried in the Savannah Tribune.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Smith and Alfred Green
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Charles Smith and Alfred Green occurred in August 1920 in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, when citizens of New Holland and Intercourse raised lynching threats against the two Black men, who were charged with robbery. Officials placed the men in the Lancaster county jail on August 9 to prevent the threats from being carried out, and no violence against them was reported.

episodes.title: Killing of Fred Minge
episodes.doubt: undated single report (before Aug. 6); killed on the lake by fellow sailors
episodes.summary: The killing of Fred Minge was the beating and drowning of a Black chef by sailors aboard the lake steamer "City of Toledo", reported from Toledo, Ohio, in August 1920. According to the only report found, the sailors attacked him after he denounced crew members who had taken part in recent riots, and threw him into the lake, where he drowned.

episodes.title: Attack on Black workers near the Granby plant, 1920
episodes.doubt: attackers described as Spanish and Mexican strikers, not white
episodes.summary: The attack on Black workers near the Granby plant was a street assault on August 9, 1920, in which a group of Spanish and Mexican men, presumably strikers, beat several Black men near Fortieth street and North Park drive in the East St. Louis area of Illinois. No casualties were reported, and three Spaniards were held after the Black men identified them.

episodes.title: Elkins street fight and arrest of Dr. Laws
episodes.doubt: street fights between individuals; paper calls it a 'race war' but no mob attack
episodes.summary: The Elkins street fight and arrest of Dr. Laws was a clash in Elkins, West Virginia, on Saturday night, 14 August 1920, in which a white man fought Dr. Laws, a Black physician. The white man was fined, Laws was then arrested and his office raided, and the local weekly called it "another race war".

episodes.title: Manhunt for Buford Monday
episodes.summary: The manhunt for Buford Monday was a search in August and September 1920 by armed posses across Madison, Jessamine and Fayette counties, Kentucky, for Buford Monday (also spelled Munday), a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Charles Sauers (also Sowers) of Valley View. Associated Press dispatches described several hundred farmers and county officers carrying guns, ropes and pitchforks, and one headline said he would be lynched if captured. No capture was reported, and the Chicago Whip, the one Black paper found to cover the case, said the alarm had been raised after Monday tipped his hat to the woman.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Annie Rodwell
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Annie Rodwell was a mob pursuit of a married Black woman in southern Georgia in August 1920, organized, according to the Phoenix Tribune, by the family of N. N. Starling, a married white man who had been seeing her. The couple escaped to Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, where both were jailed while Georgia sought their extradition, a case two Black weeklies presented as revealing Southern race relations.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sills Spinks and Juster Jennings
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sills Spinks and Juster Jennings was the shooting of two Black men by a white posse near Grimes, Dale County, Alabama, late on the night of Thursday, July 29, 1920. The posse was hunting the assailant of a white woman, and the killings were followed by beatings, a lodge-hall burning and expulsions. A grand jury investigated and warrants were reported for three white men, but no outcome appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Lawyer Tobias
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Lawyer Tobias was a mob pursuit in southeastern Kansas on August 12, 1920, after Tobias, a young Black man, was accused of shooting Howard Thomas, a white cement manufacturer, at Fort Scott. Cars of armed Fort Scott men chased the officers who moved Tobias to Pittsburg, Kansas, and then to the jail at Joplin, Missouri. Tobias was later convicted of the shooting and sent to the penitentiary.

episodes.title: West Fourteenth Street longshoremen's strike riot
episodes.summary: The West Fourteenth Street longshoremen's strike riot was a fight on the evening of August 16, 1920, in which striking white longshoremen attacked a group of Black strikebreakers near Fourteenth Street and Ninth Avenue in Manhattan, New York City. Two strikers were shot and several Black workers were injured, and police reserves dispersed the crowds before any arrests were made. New York dailies, a wire dispatch and the Black press reported it, several of them calling it a "race riot."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Anderson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Frank Anderson took place at Leesburg, Virginia, on the night of August 12-13, 1920, when Loudoun County residents stormed the county jail to seize Anderson, a Black man held on a charge of attempting to attack a young white woman. Sheriff Edwards and his deputies held the crowd off, and on the direction of Governor Westmoreland Davis, Anderson was taken to the jail at Winchester, where militia were kept ready. White papers in Washington, Richmond, Birmingham and Chattanooga carried the story as a short news item, and the Richmond Planet, a Black weekly, reprinted the Richmond account a week later.
